en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question on Inference.

4. The Question on the Departed Ancestors and Others “Venerable Nāgasena, when these donors give a gift and dedicate it to their departed ancestors, saying, ‘May this reach them,’ do they receive any result (vipāka) from that cause?
“Some, Great King, receive it; some do not receive it.”
“Who, venerable sir, obtain it, and who do not obtain it?
“Those reborn in hell, great king, do not obtain it; those gone to heaven do not obtain it; those gone to the animal realm do not obtain it;
and among the four types of *petas*, three types of *petas* do not obtain it: those who eat vomit, those who suffer from hunger and thirst, and those who subsist on the foam of boiled rice.”
“Tormented by thirst, the *petas* who subsist on what is given by others obtain [food] only when they are remembered.
“If that is so, venerable Nāgasena, then the gift of the donors becomes withered and fruitless, if those for whose sake it was made do not receive it?
“Certainly not, Great King. That gift is neither fruitless nor without result; the donors themselves experience its fruit.”
“Therefore, venerable Nāgasena, convince me by means of that reason.
“In this case, Great King, suppose some people, having prepared fish, meat, liquor, cooked rice, and various snacks, were going to a family of relatives;
if those relatives were not to accept that gift, would that gift have withered away?”
“Would it go away or perish?
“Certainly not, venerable sir; that belongs to the owners themselves.
“In the same way, great king, only the donors experience the fruit of that gift.”
“But just as, great king, if a man has entered a womb, in the absence of an exit-way in front, by what way would he emerge?
“By the very same way he entered, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, it is the donors themselves who experience the fruit of that gift.”
“Very well, venerable Nāgasena; it is so, and I accept it as such: the givers alone experience the fruit of that gift, and we do not contradict that principle.

“But, venerable Nāgasena, if the gift given by these donors reaches the deceased ancestors and they experience its result, then what of one who is a killer of living beings—cruel, bloody-handed, and of corrupt intention—who, having slain humans, performs a terrible [deed]?”
“If one were to perform an act of merit and dedicate it to the deceased ancestors, saying,
‘May the fruit of this act of mine accrue to the deceased ancestors,’ would that fruit then accrue to them?
“Certainly not, Great King.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the cause there, what is the reason, by which one attains the wholesome and does not attain the unwholesome?
“This is not a question that should be asked, Great King. Do not ask what should not be asked just because you think there must be an answerer.
Why is space without support? Why does the Ganges not flow upwards? Why is it that these people [behave as they do]?”
“Whether they be birds, bipeds, deer, or quadrupeds”—you will ask me even about that.
“I do not ask you, venerable Nāgasena, out of a desire to trouble you; rather, I ask for the sake of dispelling my doubt.
There are many people in the world who follow wrong paths and lack vision; [I ask] so that they may find no opportunity to gain an advantage over you.”
“Thus I ask you this.
“It is not possible, Great King, to share out an evil deed with one who has neither done it nor consented to it.

Just as people, Great King, can carry away water even from a very great distance by means of a water-scoop, could a massive, solid rock mountain be carried away as desired by means of a scoop, Great King?”
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, it is possible to share wholesome states, but it is not possible to share unwholesome states.
Or again, great king, just as it is possible to light a lamp with oil, could one, great king, light a lamp with water?”
“No indeed, Bhante.
“In the same way, Great King, it is possible to share out what is wholesome, but it is not possible to share out what is unwholesome.
Or again, Great King, just as farmers take water from a reservoir and ripen their crops, would it be possible, Great King, to take water from the great ocean and ripen one’s crops?”
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, it is possible to share wholesome states, but it is not possible to share unwholesome states.
“Venerable Nāgasena, for what reason is it possible to share wholesome states, but not possible to share unwholesome states?”
“Convince me with a reason; I am not blind or without light—I shall know it by hearing.

“Great King, the unwholesome is little, while the wholesome is much. Because it is little, the unwholesome merely consumes its doer; because it is much, the wholesome overwhelms the world together with its devas.
“Give me an illustration.”
“Great king, suppose a single small drop of water were to fall upon the earth; would that drop of water, great king, spread over ten or even twelve leagues?
“No, venerable sir; it would simply be absorbed right where that drop of water fell.
“For what reason, great king?”
“Because the drop of water is small, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, a small unwholesome deed, because it is small, consumes only the doer; it cannot be shared out.
Or again, great king, suppose a vast great cloud were to rain down, saturating the surface of the earth—would that great cloud, great king, overflow on all sides?”

“Yes, venerable sir, having filled it, that great cloud would overspread even ten or twelve leagues with its pools, springs, rivers, branches, caves, gullies, lakes, wells, lotus ponds, and water reservoirs.
“For what reason, Great King?
“Because of the greatness of the cloud, venerable sir.”
“In the same way, Great King, wholesome action is abundant; because it is so abundant, it can be shared even among gods and humans.
“Venerable Nāgasena, for what reason is unwholesome action slight and wholesome action more abundant?
“In this case, Great King, whoever gives a gift, undertakes moral discipline, or performs the observance-day duties—”
He becomes elated, overjoyed, laughing, delighted, serene in mind, and filled with rapture;
in him, rapture arises again and again. For one whose mind is full of rapture, wholesome states increase more and more.

Great King, it is just as if water were entering by one side and exiting by another from a well completely filled with water; even as it exits, it arises again and again, and it is impossible to bring it to exhaustion.
In the same way, Great King, wholesome merit increases more and more.
Even if a man were to reflect upon the wholesome he has performed for a hundred years, Great King, with each reflection, that wholesome merit increases further and further.
It is possible for him to share that wholesome merit with whomever he wishes; this, Great King, is the reason why wholesome merit is so abundant.
But when one performs an unwholesome deed, O Great King, one later becomes remorseful;
the mind of the remorseful person shrinks back, recoils, turns away, and does not expand; it sorrows, burns, wastes away, and perishes;
it does not grow, but is consumed right there.

"Just as, great king, when there is a dry riverbed with a vast expanse of sand that is uneven, undulating, and winding, the little water that comes flowing over it diminishes, wastes away, does not increase, and is exhausted right there;
even so, great king, for one who performs unwholesome deeds, the mind recoils, shrinks back, turns away, and does not expand;
it sorrows, burns, diminishes, wastes away, does not increase, and is exhausted right there."
“This, O Great King, is the reason why unwholesome action is slight.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
The fourth question, concerning the departed ancestors and so forth, is concluded.
